It is only fair to mention here the modern Arab scholar Jabbūr ʿAbd al-Nūr of Lebanon. He managed to see through this ambiguity in the Brethren’s texts and identify their real position in their discussion of the influence of the planets and celestial spheres on the material world. He writes: “At times they do not fail to say, by way of concealment and precaution, that God determines the fate of universals and particulars. Yet their real opinion is clear and can be seen by any reader in most of the Rasāʾil. They believe that the planets are the direct cause of natural generation, the appearance of matter and form, their development into mineral, plant, animal, and human forms, and the emergence of individuality within species.” See Dr. Jabbūr ʿAbd al-Nūr, Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ, Dār al-Maʿārif, Egypt, 1954, p. 28.↩︎

This hierarchy of the human path to knowledge is close to Hegel’s three-stage account of coming to know the truth. First comes a primitive clarity gained through the senses. Then comes correct knowledge of a thing or proposition, such as knowing that 2 × 2 = 4; this is higher than the first stage. Finally comes the level at which knowledge uncovers a general law of nature or society, such as the law of gravity. This means that the Brethren of Purity—or science and philosophy together in their time—had an idea close to what we now regard as true: that human beings discover truth gradually, moving from simple and primitive knowledge to complex knowledge whose correctness can be established, and then to objective truth itself as it appears in the form of a law.↩︎

See Rasāʾil, vol. 1, p. 105. In this passage, however, the Brethren exempt “thoughts, revelation, and inspiration” from the need for evidence. They say that knowledge obtained through these does not come through acquired learning but is a gift from God. Yet in the earlier passage they made thoughts, revelation, and inspiration subject to the activity of the thinking faculty, which acquires its information from the sensible world rather than receiving it as a gift from God. Is this contradiction in the first volume of the Rasāʾil deliberate concealment and taqiyya—a kind of “tactic”? Or is it one of the contradictions that any thinker is bound to fall into when one foot stands on the ground of philosophical idealism and the other on the ground of philosophical materialism, whether consciously or spontaneously?↩︎

Everything said here about “examples” and “counterparts” is quoted from Jāmiʿat al-Jāmiʿa of the Rasāʾil, ch. 6, p. 76. The final phrase about “the human form, which is the perfection of natural bodies and sensible individuals,” clearly has an Aristotelian background. When this Aristotelian element is joined to the wider argument of the Brethren in this passage, the Platonic and Aristotelian elements merge into a new theoretical form independent of both Plato and Aristotle. This fits the general philosophical direction of the Brethren’s encyclopedia: a new form of objective idealism.↩︎

It may be said that the Brethren of Purity also looked down on the material world. They speak of “purifying” the soul of bodily needs and desires so that after death it will deserve to join the Universal Soul, where its paradise and eternal happiness lie; this is how they interpret paradise. But despising matter in this sense is very different from denying that the material world exists. The Stoics, for example, also looked down on the material world while at the same time recognizing its objective existence.↩︎
